input:
## Scope

Gas drying, which involves the removal of water vapour from a gas stream before the stream is compressed, transported, or processed further, is a mature and widely practised operation, and the adsorbents that perform the work are silica gel, activated alumina, and the molecular sieves. The present review covers a total of 143 papers published over the last 6 years. The quantities that the papers report include the equilibrium uptake of water, the dew point of the dried gas, the regeneration conditions, and the life of the bed in service. Papers have been included where the feed carries water as the principal adsorbate, while mixed feeds with competing adsorbates are treated only where the water results can be separated out in a satisfactory manner.

## Established results

It is well established that water adsorbs on all three material classes in preference to the permanent gases, and the dried gas leaves the bed at a dew point that is set by the state of the bed at the end of the adsorption step. Equilibrium uptake rises steeply at low partial pressure in the case of the molecular sieves and rather more gradually in the case of silica gel, so that the sieves hold their capacity into the driest part of the duty and are duly chosen where the dew point specification is severe. Activated alumina, for its part, sits somewhere between the two in uptake behaviour and is widely used where the specification is moderate and the feed is rough.

Regeneration is accomplished by heating the bed, by reducing the pressure, or by a combination of the two, and the completeness of the regeneration effectively sets the working capacity of the next cycle. Working capacity falls as the feed temperature rises, because the equilibrium moves against adsorption, and it likewise falls as regeneration is shortened or cooled. The pressure drop across a bed of pellets and the heat released on adsorption are reported consistently enough across the literature that neither is a live dispute: the real disagreements, as will be seen, lie elsewhere.

## Disagreements

Reports are in conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. For what is nominally the same material, one laboratory's isotherm lies well above another's in exactly the region that fixes the dew point, and the dried-gas performance that a designer would calculate from the two isotherms differs accordingly. It should be emphasised that the conflict does not resolve into a simple error. Pretreatment differs between laboratories, and a bed that is dried harder before the measurement starts from a different state; the measurement itself also differs, being gravimetric in one laboratory and by breakthrough in another, and the two routes weight the slow part of the uptake in quite different ways. Sample history, moreover, is reported too unevenly to allow the matter to be settled from the published record.

A smaller disagreement runs alongside the main one. Some reports treat the uptake at low partial pressure as a property of the material alone, while other reports show it moving with the binder and the forming route, which would make it a property of the manufactured pellet rather than of the crystal or gel. The distinction is by no means a trivial one for specification: a designer buying on the first view accepts any pellet of the named material, whereas on the second view the pellet itself must be specified.

## Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is the uptake retained after many regeneration cycles. Papers routinely give the fresh capacity, and a smaller number give the capacity after a mere handful of cycles, but the bed in service is regenerated hundreds of times between change-outs, and its working capacity late in life is precisely the figure that a design actually consumes. Ageing under a real feed, with its trace contaminants arriving cycle after cycle, is reported hardly at all in the literature.

This gap is far from being a mere detail. A drying unit is sized on working capacity, and if that capacity decays over the course of the bed's life, the dew point specification is duly met when the bed is new and missed well before the bed is changed. Until such time as retained uptake over long cycling is measured and published, designs will continue to carry the decay as an allowance rather than as a datum, and the allowance differs from designer to designer because the literature gives it nothing solid to rest on.

The three classes are treated separately throughout, because their uptake behaviour, regeneration, and failure modes differ enough that a pooled account would hide the disagreements the review exists to record.

## Established results

Water adsorbs on all three material classes in preference to the permanent gases, and the dried gas leaves the bed at a dew point set by the state of the bed at the end of the adsorption step. Equilibrium uptake rises steeply at low partial pressure for the molecular sieves and more gradually for silica gel, so the sieves hold their capacity into the driest part of the duty and are chosen where the dew point specification is severe. The pressure drop across a bed of pellets and the heat released on adsorption are reported consistently enough across the literature that neither is a live dispute: the disagreements lie elsewhere.

The heat released on adsorption raises the temperature of the bed during the adsorption step and works against uptake until the heat is carried away, so beds are cycled with a cooling or purge stage where the duty allows. The temperature excursion of the bed is one of the quantities on which reports agree closely, because it follows from the isotherm and the heat capacity of the bed rather than from any contested measurement.

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. Sample history is reported too unevenly to settle the matter from the published record. Until pretreatment and measurement route are reported as standard, the conflict will persist in the literature, because each new isotherm is measured from a different starting state and the differences are absorbed into the material's name.

A smaller disagreement runs alongside the main one. Some reports treat the uptake at low partial pressure as a property of the material alone, while others show it moving with the binder and the forming route, which would make it a property of the manufactured pellet rather than the crystal or gel. The distinction matters for specification: a designer buying on the first view accepts any pellet of the named material, and on the second view must specify the pellet.

The measurement nobody reports is the uptake retained after many regeneration cycles. Papers give the fresh capacity, and a smaller number give the capacity after a handful of cycles, but the bed in service is regenerated hundreds of times between change-outs, and its working capacity late in life is the figure a design actually consumes. Ageing under a real feed, with its trace contaminants arriving cycle after cycle, is reported hardly at all.

A second gap runs with the first: no standard ageing protocol exists. Without an agreed cycle of humidity, temperature, and contaminant exposure, the few retention figures that do exist cannot be compared between laboratories, and each stands alone. Operators bridge the gap with the bed life a vendor will guarantee, which transfers the missing measurement into a commercial term rather than closing it.

The gap is not a detail. A drying unit is sized on working capacity, and if that capacity decays over the bed's life, the dew point specification is met when the bed is new and missed before the bed is changed. Until retained uptake over long cycling is measured and published, designs carry the decay as an allowance rather than a datum, and the allowance differs from designer to designer because the literature gives it nothing to rest on.
